transcript.text: Outcome: Calculate output per worker and interpret productivity changes.

Labor productivity measures output per worker or per hour worked. For example, 2,400 units produced in 300 labor hours means 2,400 / 300 = 8 units per hour. Productivity compares output with the labor input used to produce it, so changes in both output and labor matter. A country can consume more when its workers produce more output per worker.
Measure labor productivity as real output per worker or per hour worked.
Use the same output and labor units when comparing periods.
An increase in total output need not raise productivity if labor input also rises.
Do not confuse total output with output per unit of labor. Productivity compares output with the labor input used to produce it, so changes in both output and labor matter.

A workshop produces 2,400 units using 300 labor hours, so productivity is 2,400 / 300 = 8 units per hour. Next month it produces 2,700 units using the same 300 hours: 9 units per hour. Productivity rises by (9 - 8) / 8 x 100 = 12.5%. More output per labor hour, not simply more total hours, is the improvement.
A business uses more labor hours but produces the same amount of output. What happens to labor productivity?
Return to the game and master this concept.

transcript.text: Outcome: Evaluate policies affecting long-run productivity and growth.

Long-run growth policy raises productive capacity rather than current spending alone. Saving and reliable finance support capital formation; education builds human capital; research and competition can advance technology. Stable property rights and institutions make firms more willing to invest. Because physical capital faces diminishing returns, sustained growth usually depends on several of these channels working together.
The policy changes capital formation, human capital, technology, or institutions.
The question distinguishes productive capacity from a temporary demand increase.
Reliable finance and property rights affect whether saving becomes productive investment.
The proposed change can raise output per worker over time.

Do not treat a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity. Long-run growth policy works through productivity, capital formation, human capital, technology, and institutions.
WORKED EXAMPLE: EVALUATING A GROWTH POLICY

A government compares a temporary shopping rebate with worker training and reliable electricity for firms. The rebate can raise current spending, but training can improve skills and reliable power can reduce lost production. For long-run growth, evaluate the latter policies by their likely productivity gains, resource costs, implementation quality, and time to deliver results.
Why might worker training raise long-run productive capacity while a temporary shopping rebate mainly changes current demand?

transcript.text: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
Outcome: Analyze Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade.

Comparative advantage belongs to the producer with the lower opportunity cost, even when another producer has an absolute advantage in both goods. Compute the forgone alternative per unit, then select the lower opportunity cost. Specialization creates potential output gains; the trading terms determine whether both sides gain. Use opportunity cost and net benefits to evaluate specialization and exchange. Different opportunity costs create room for specialization and mutually beneficial exchange.
Use opportunity cost and net benefits to evaluate specialization and exchange.
Different opportunity costs create room for specialization and mutually beneficial exchange.
One lamp costs Ari 2 rugs and costs Bea 6 rugs.
One producer is more productive in both goods.
Two firms specialize and create 40 extra units of combined output.

A common mistake is to choose the producer with the greatest absolute output. Comparative advantage depends on lower opportunity cost, and a mutually beneficial terms-of-trade ratio lies between the two opportunity costs.

Ari gives up 24/12 = 2 rugs per lamp; Bea gives up 60/10 = 6 rugs per lamp. Ari has comparative advantage in lamps. For rugs, Bea gives up 1/6 lamp, below Ari's 1/2 lamp. A trade of one lamp for four rugs lies between the two lamp costs, so both can gain from specializing and exchanging.
If 1 X costs 2 Y, what is the cost of 1 Y?
